questions.question: Why might a version-control tool let you undo most mistakes, even though a wrong command feels like it could destroy work?
How should you choose between rewriting history and adding a new commit to undo a mistake, depending on whether others have your commits?
What would you expect a tool to need to keep so that a commit nobody points to anymore can still be recovered, and what limits that?
In Git, why can you undo most mistakes even though a wrong command feels like it could destroy your work?
questions.answer: Git keeps almost everything you commit for weeks, and each kind of mistake has its own undo. A change always sits in the working tree, the index or the history, and undo commands just move a change between these places or move a branch along the history. Only edits that were never committed are truly lost.
rubric: Git keeps committed work for a long time (via the history and reflog)
Each kind of mistake has its own undo command
Undo commands only move changes between working tree, index and history, or move a branch
Uncommitted, unstaged edits are the main thing that can really be lost
questions.why: faithful: 'Only edits that were never committed are truly lost' overstates the source, which says restore is 'one of the few' losing commands and that unreachable commits can be garbage-collected after the reflog expires.

questions.question: In Git, how do you choose between `git reset` and `git revert` to undo a commit, depending on whether others already have it?
questions.answer: If the commit is not shared yet, use reset to step the branch back, since nobody else holds the old history. Once others have pulled it, use revert: reset moves the branch and leaves their copies disagreeing with yours, while revert adds a new commit that is the exact opposite of the bad one, so history only grows and nobody's copy is contradicted. The cost is a visible record of the mistake.
rubric: Reset moves the branch, so others' histories disagree with yours
Revert adds an opposite commit, so history only grows, at the cost of a visible record

questions.question: In Git, how can you recover a commit that no branch points to any more, such as one left by an amend or a hard reset?
questions.answer: Every time HEAD moves (commit, reset, checkout, amend), Git writes a line in the reflog, a private log of where HEAD has been. Run `git reflog`, find the entry for the lost commit, and move back to it, for example with `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`.
rubric: The reflog records every HEAD movement
Use `git reflog` to find the entry for the lost commit
Return to it, e.g. `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`

questions.question: In Git, which command takes a file out of the index but keeps your edits on disk?
In Git, how do the three modes of `git reset` differ in what happens to the changes from the commits you step over?
questions.answer: `--soft` leaves the changes in the index, ready to commit again. `--mixed` (the default) leaves them in the working tree, unstaged. `--hard` removes them from both, so files look as they did at the commit you reset to.
rubric: --soft keeps changes staged in the index
--mixed (default) keeps them in the working tree, unstaged
--hard removes them from index and working tree

questions.question: In Git, by default the reflog keeps its entries for ____ (30 days for entries of commits no branch can reach).
questions.why: worth_it: the exact default expiry is trivia; what matters is that the reflog expires and is local, which this card doesn't test.

questions.question: In Git, what is a detached HEAD?
questions.answer: A state where HEAD points straight at a commit instead of at a branch, e.g. after checking out a commit by hash or a tag. Commits made there belong to no branch; make one with `git switch -c <name>` to keep them.
questions.why: one_target: a short 'what is' card whose answer also has to cover causes, the consequence and the `git switch -c` fix.
